spans.s:
Paṅkti, originally a ‘set of five,’ denotes as early as the Rigveda a ‘series’ generally. In the taittirīya Āraṇyaka the word is used of the series of a man's ancestors whom he purifies by certain conduct.
Foot notes x. 117, 8, as taken by the St. Petersburg Dictionary.
x. 38, 39.

Pāṃsu in the Atharvaveda and later denotes ‘dust’ or ‘sand,’ usually in the plural. Among the portents enumerated in the Adbhuta brāhmaṇa is a rain of dust or sand (pāṃsuvarṣa), a phenomenon not rare in India.
Foot notes vii. 109, 2; xii. 1, 26.
taittirīya brāhmaṇa, ii. 6, 10, 2; nirukta, xii. 19, etc.
vi. 8 (Indische Studien, 1, 40). Cf. Varāhamihira, Bṛhatsaṃhitā, xxii. 6.
The adjective pāṃsura is found in Rv. i. 22, 17, with a variant, pāṃsula, sāmaveda, i. 3, 1, 3, 9. Cf. Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, iv. 5, 1, 9.

Pāṅktra is the name of an animal mentioned in the list of victims at the aśvamedha, or ‘horse-sacrifice,’ in the yajurveda Saṃhitās. The ‘field-rat’ seems to be meant.
Foot notes Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā, iii. 14, 7; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, xxiv. 26. Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 85.

Pāna, ‘drink,’ occurs in the Śatapatha brāhmaṇa and the Upaniṣads.
Foot notes xiii. 4, 2, 17.
Bṛhadāraṇyaka upaniṣad, iv. 1, 43; Chāndogya upaniṣad, viii. 2, 7, etc.

Pānta occurs several times in the Rigveda, apparently meaning ‘drink,’ ‘beverage’ (cf. pāna). Geldner, however, thinks that in one passage^4 pānta is the name of a prince.
Foot notes i. 122, 1; 155, 1; viii. 92, 1; ix. 65, 28 (a very doubtful passage); x. 88, 1.
So nirukta, vii. 25; Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, s.v.; Oldenberg, ṛgveda-Noten, 1, 122, 123.
Vedische Studien, 2, 139; Rigveda, Glossar, 108.

Pān-nejana in the Śatapatha brāhmaṇa denotes a ‘vessel for washing the feet.’
Foot notes iii. 8, 2, 1; 9, 3, 27; xiii. 5, 2, 1.
